description: ITHERYON is named after an imagined civilization for which a star is a power source and building worlds is ordinary engineering. We are curious about space exploration, physics and future technologies, and we turn ambitious questions into interactive projects grounded in real data. We welcome web development, 3D, UI/UX, physics, astronomy, data analysis and storytelling skills. We value curiosity, honest feedback and initiative.
summary:
Mission ʻOumuamua is a browser game about sending a probe after the first known interstellar visitor. You choose a route, build the spacecraft and fly its critical manoeuvres before trying to photograph the encounter.

Getting there is only part of the job. Your camera, power supply, memory and radio determine what you can observe, keep and send home. After the flyby, you choose which data to transmit first and see what reaches Earth, then change the design and try again.

The game connects NASA's four mission segments: user, space, launch and ground. Published Project Lyra routes and NASA/JPL data support the teaching model; the encounter includes a fictional discovery.
details:
The mission begins with a scientific question: do you want to study the object's shape and surface, investigate its composition, or collect evidence to compare ideas about its origin? You then choose a route and set the Deep Space Network support, including antenna hours per week and the years available to send data home.

There are eight route options. Seven come from Project Lyra papers; some cannot carry the proposed mission, for the reasons given in those papers. "Direct to ʻOumuamua" is a teaching option that fails under the game's assumptions. Its explanation introduces the gravity assists and Jupiter burn used by the published routes.

In the spacecraft builder, you select a camera, spectrometer, radioisotope power unit, antenna and recorder. Each change updates the mass, power and budget checks. If the design cannot launch, the game explains the constraint. A strip connects the four NASA mission segments, while a teaching scale based on JPL Concept Maturity Levels tracks the checks you have satisfied. That scale is a game model.

The chosen route determines the flight stages. You fly the launch window and planetary encounters by hand, adjusting the aim point at Venus or Earth and timing the Jupiter Oberth burn near closest approach. The flyby curve responds to your input and shows the consequences of passing too close or too far away. A blink-comparison search asks you to pick out a faint moving target beyond the Kuiper belt, inspired by the search for Arrokoth during the New Horizons mission.

At ʻOumuamua, you steer the camera to record the encounter. Only frames you capture can enter the stored and transmitted record. Back on Earth, the result shows the scientific goal's full, partial or failed outcome, the deciding constraint, and how much data you collected, kept and received. Recalculated advice suggests design changes, and retry keeps the previous attempt for comparison.

A larger recorder can preserve more observations while leaving the amount received on Earth unchanged if the radio link is the limiting factor. Comparing attempts lets the player see why a change helped, or why it did not.

The model evaluates spacecraft designs in TypeScript. NASA/JPL Horizons supplies positions and distances, and the Project Lyra papers supply route dates, speeds and delivered masses. The planetary encounters use hyperbolic relations with values from NASA fact sheets. On-screen source tags identify published figures (PAPER), NASA data (NASA), physical calculations (PHYSICS) and teaching assumptions (MODEL). The inhabitants inside ʻOumuamua are fictional.

The game uses React, TypeScript, Vite and three.js, with tests run by Node's test runner. It runs in the browser without an application backend or tracking.

Play: https://mission-oumuamua.vercel.app/ · Source code (MIT): https://github.com/MikeLenval/mission-oumuamua
